Carmen is 40, works as sales manager, with partner or family.

How life is going overall. good.

What brings them here now. Carmen Watson, a 40-year-old sales manager, presents with roughly two months of escalating work stress following a leadership change that raised her regional target by thirty percent, replaced her forecasting process with an unfamiliar live dashboard, and made Monday pipeline calls a weekly test of her numbers; she describes constant worry, Sunday-night dread, and a sense that her careful systems no longer protect her. She also reports secondary friction at home, where her partner of eleven years has told her she is 'there but not there' and their conversation has thinned to logistics since a sharp exchange in March. She denies any decline in her performance or her team's results, denies changes in sleep or appetite beyond feeling 'wound up' on Sunday nights, denies increased alcohol use and any thoughts of self-harm, and her routines — work, garden, knitting, volunteering — have continued largely intact.
What they want out of support: I want to get my Sundays back — to stop spending them dreading Monday — and to be able to tell Daniel honestly how work is going instead of saying it's just a busy quarter.

Predisposing. Carmen grew up in a steady, orderly Connecticut household where affection was never in doubt but attention had to be earned: her father, a municipal engineer, went over her homework in red pen and once asked, without unkindness, what had happened to the other six points on a 94. Nothing she did wrong was ever punished — it was simply corrected and folded into the next expectation, so that doing something well mainly meant a harder thing was coming. She learned to be the one who had it handled, and by the time she left for college she had never once arrived anywhere unprepared. What she never learned was how to feel finished.

Precipitating. About ten weeks ago the company brought in a new VP of sales from outside, 'to shake things up,' who raised the regional target by thirty percent, retired Carmen's carefully built quarterly forecasting cadence in favor of a live dashboard nobody had been trained on, and has opened every Monday since by asking her, in front of her peers, to justify her numbers. Her title, reviews, and results have not changed, but the ground moved: five years of dependable process is now 'legacy thinking,' and the regional director track she had mapped for herself runs through a man who measures her in weekly increments. She started opening the dashboard before her coffee, circled the Monday deck all week without touching it and then rebuilt it three times on Sunday, and let the Sunday hikes slide for a few weeks. Three weeks ago, after the fourth such Monday, she snapped at Daniel over the gutters — 'a nothing,' she calls it — and though Friday dinners have continued, some evenings have felt flat; she decided to reach out after spending an entire Saturday at her desk re-running forecast scenarios instead of in the garden, and did not like what that told her about where this was heading.

Perpetuating. Everything she does is aimed at never being caught unprepared and never being caught struggling; the first eats her weekends and thins her sleep, the second starves the one relationship that would hold her, and together they keep the worry fed because none of it gets said out loud until it comes out sharp.
- overpreparation: She circles the Monday pipeline deck all week without opening it, then builds it on Saturday, revises it Sunday morning, and rebuilds it from scratch Sunday night 'just to be sure,' rehearsing answers to questions the new VP has never asked. The second version is always good enough; the third costs her the Sunday hike and buys about an hour of feeling ready.
- going_over_it: On the drive home she replays the Monday call interchange by interchange, matching what was said against what she should have said, and some nights she is still re-reading the forecast thread on her phone at eleven, running numbers she already checked at nine. Nothing new ever turns up; she checks anyway.
- hiding_needs: She has told Daniel it's 'a busy quarter, it'll settle' enough times that he has stopped asking twice, and she steers their evenings toward logistics — the gutters, his mother's birthday — because saying she is struggling at work would mean admitting she isn't handling it. The sharp exchange in March started exactly there.

Protective. The shape of Carmen's week still holds — knitting most evenings, the garden on Saturday mornings, her first-Thursday shift organizing the Ridgefield library's community reads, a Sunday hike when the weather allows. Her circle is small but durable: Daniel still cooks Friday nights and has taken to leaving the crossword half-finished for her, and her younger sister Beth calls every Sunday no matter how many times Carmen says she's busy. And she still trusts her own hands at the work itself — put a struggling rep with a stuck deal in front of her and she is patient, steady, and exactly the coach she has always been; it is the one room where the worry goes quiet.
